headline: Oil Stockpiling to Influence Market in 2027, Energy Aspects Says
author: Rong Wei Neo and Weilun Soon

paragraphs.text: Rong Wei Neo and Weilun Soon
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 1:31 AM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Oil stockpiling will be important factor for the next couple of years, potentially tightening the market and aiding prices even with a projected global surplus, according to Energy Aspects Ltd.

Around 600 million barrels of inventories have been drawn down worldwide since the start of the Middle East war, so there's a need to rebuild, said Amrita Sen, founder and director of the consultancy.

China will be the biggest stockpiler, and will add 160 million barrels of new storage capacity this year and next, she said in a Bloomberg TV interview. Beijing is already refilling inventories, plus the US is set to rebuild strategic stockpiles at a low level from the second quarter of 2027, Sen said.

Refiners in China, the world's No. 1 oil importer, have boosted purchases this month, taking advantage of falling prices. Global benchmark Brent has plunged over the last few months as Persian Gulf exports recovered despite continued Iranian attacks on shipping. Energy Aspects is forecasting a global surplus of 1.2 million barrels a day next year.

Traders are "getting very complacent" and want to short oil, but they're doing so at their own risk when stockpiles are low and the chance of production outages is high, Sen said, referring to recent incidents in Brazil and Norway. Refilling stockpiles would take time, she said.
"Inventory refilling is a multiyear story, with 2028 being the bigger one than 2027 especially as the conflict continues for the first half at least."

Exporting Persian Gulf oil is likely to remain costly and inefficient, with higher freight costs effectively baked into the trade, Sen said. Logistics, rather than production capacity, may become the biggest constraint, she said in a separate interview, adding that Energy Aspects was seeing Iraq deferring loadings by more than a week, while ship-to-ship transfers and uncertainty around Hormuz transits create further friction.
"From a geopolitical point of view, we think this current status quo is the new reality," Sen said in the TV interview.
